input:
Current use

Electricity use at the mill currently amounts to 1423 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share; the remainder is spread across the mill's various drives, pumps, fans, and auxiliary services, none of which approaches the refrigeration load in scale. This figure is a metered annual total, and it serves as the base against which every saving identified in this assessment is expressed: a measure that saves a given share of electricity is credited with that share of the 1423 MWh, and no other base is used at any point. Steam is accounted for separately, in the steam section below, because its figures are drawn from a different record and cover a considerably shorter period. The assessment covers the site as metered: electricity generated on site, where such generation occurs, enters the figures through the same meters, and no attempt has been made to separate purchased and generated electricity within the totals that are used here. The annual total itself is built up from monthly meter readings, and it consequently smooths the seasons out of the site's demand: a heavy winter month and a light summer month enter the average side by side, which is the appropriate basis for measures whose savings likewise run throughout the year. Measures whose effect is essentially seasonal are not credited on this base, and none is assessed here.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the mill. The plant supplies chilled water and cold air both to the process and to the stores, and it operates throughout the year, which is an important part of the explanation for the size of its share of the annual total: a load that runs in every month of the year inevitably accumulates more energy than a heavier load that runs for only part of it. Refrigeration is also the point at which the heat leaves the system. A refrigeration plant works by moving heat from the cooled spaces to its condensers and rejecting it at that point, and at present that rejected heat is simply discharged without being used. The heat-recovery retrofit that is assessed here would take heat from the discharge side of the refrigeration plant and return it to duties that currently draw on other sources. The saving that is projected is a saving of electricity: the recovered heat displaces work that would otherwise be done elsewhere in the mill's systems, and the assessment accordingly credits the retrofit with 15% of electricity use, corresponding to a derived saving of 213 MWh per year. It should be noted that this projection is a calculation based on the rated duty of the plant and its running hours, rather than a measurement of any kind; it rests on the assumption that the recovered heat will in fact be taken up whenever the plant is running, and a duty that is unable to accept heat at the times when the plant rejects it would inevitably return a smaller saving. It is also relevant that the heat rejected by the plant is low-grade in character: it is warm rather than hot, and it is therefore suited to duties that require warmth rather than high temperature, such as the heating of water and of air and the preheating of streams on their way to hotter duties. The mill possesses duties of this kind in every season, although their size varies with the weather, and it is the match between rejection and demand, considered hour by hour, that the projection assumes and that the design stage will have to test.

Steam

Steam serves the drying section together with the mill's space and process heating requirements. The steam figures that appear in the mill's records are drawn from one winter month, and this limitation deserves to be stated plainly. Winter is the season in which steam demand is at its heaviest: the incoming water and air are at their coldest, the heating load reaches its highest level, and the drying section is working against the coldest feed of the year. A figure taken from such a month, if it were read as a yearly figure, would overstate steam use across the year as a whole, and any saving expressed as a share of that month would overstate the saving itself in exactly the same way. For this reason, the steam section of this assessment quotes no annual steam total and ranks no steam-side measure: the available data support a statement about the winter month and about nothing beyond it. It is not that steam measures are dismissed by this limitation; rather, they are deferred by it. The metering installation that produced the winter figure remains in place, and a run of monthly figures extending across a full year would place steam on much the same footing as electricity, at which point steam-side measures could be costed and ranked against the refrigeration retrofit on a single consistent basis. The same caution would apply to any attempt to read the winter figure as representing a peak: the month in question was an ordinary working month rather than an extreme one, and nothing in the existing record serves to separate the contribution of the weather to the demand from the contribution of the production rate. Until monthly figures are available, even the direction of a steam saving is difficult to state with confidence, since a measure that saves steam in the winter may save comparatively little in the summer, when the load that it serves is smaller.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the refrigeration heat-recovery retrofit be taken forward to detailed design, with the site energy manager as the designated owner. The capital cost of the scheme is $405k. At a price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $25614, giving a derived simple payback of 15.8 years: the mill would be spending $405k in order to gain $25614 in each year, and the trade-off, stated in a single sentence, is a large capital sum set against a relatively small annual return. This is a long payback, and it should be emphasised that the recommendation is for design work, and not for immediate construction; the design stage is precisely where the principal assumption underlying the projection will be tested, namely the assumption that duties genuinely exist which are able to take the recovered heat at the times when the refrigeration plant is rejecting it. Should that assumption turn out to fail in part, the saving would fall below 213 MWh per year and the payback would lengthen beyond the figure stated above, and any decision to proceed to construction should then be taken on the basis of the design-stage numbers, rather than on the projection as it is restated here. The electricity base upon which the decision rests is, by contrast, firm: 1423 MWh per year, fully metered. The steam side of the mill's energy use is not yet ready for the same kind of treatment. The steam figures are drawn from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal in nature: no steam measure is recommended in this assessment, and the appropriate next step in relation to steam is the assembly of a full year of monthly figures, after which steam measures can be ranked against the retrofit on the same consistent basis. Two conditions are attached to the design work that is recommended. The first is that the heat sinks be confirmed at the times when the refrigeration plant actually rejects its heat, across the seasons of the year and not merely in the season in which the assessment was carried out. The second is that the capital figure be re-priced at the conclusion of the design stage, so that the eventual decision on construction is taken on the basis of a current price and a tested saving, with the payback recomputed on both of those foundations.
